title: Big-Button Amplified Phones for Hearing and Vision: Corded vs. Cordless
subtitle: How amplified home phones make calls louder and easier to dial, and how the Clarity P300 and two VTech models compare.
excerpt: If phone calls have started to sound muffled or the buttons feel too small, an amplified big-button phone may help. Here is how they work, what they cannot do, and three models to compare.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: For many people, the home phone is still the line to family, doctors and old friends. But when voices start to sound faint, or the number keys blur together, a simple call can turn into a chore. You ask people to repeat themselves, or you dial the wrong number twice.

An amplified big-button phone is built for exactly this. It makes the caller's voice louder, gives you larger keys that are easier to see and press, and often lets you call favorite people with one touch on a photo. It is a modest gadget, but for the right person it can make calls pleasant again. A note on our approach: we have not tested these phones hands-on. This article is based on what the makers, sellers and official sources publish.

These phones boost the sound coming through the handset, measured in decibels (dB, a unit of loudness). Most also have a much louder ringer, so you are less likely to miss a call from the next room, plus tone control to make voices clearer rather than just louder.

Many are also hearing-aid compatible, often marked "HAC." The FCC's consumer guide notes that hearing aid users often face noise on the phone. HAC phones are meant to cut unwanted noise and to work with a telecoil, the small coil in some hearing aids that picks up the phone's signal directly. The FCC says wireline phones must be hearing-aid compatible, and that internet-based (VoIP) wireline phones made or imported on or after February 28, 2020 must be too. The Hearing Loss Association of America says only some VoIP landline handsets are hearing-aid compatible, so it suggests looking for the HAC stamp on the packaging before you buy.

One thing to be clear about: an amplified phone is not a hearing aid. It only makes the call louder. It will not help with conversation across the dinner table, the TV or a busy restaurant. If hearing has changed, an audiologist or your doctor is the right first stop. And if reading what the caller says would help more than volume, a captioned phone is a better fit.

A corded phone stays put on a desk or wall. Clarity's own page says its P300 keeps working when the power is out. Cordless phones let you carry the handset around the house, but the base needs power. If your home loses power often, that difference matters. VTech also makes a corded/cordless hybrid, the SN5147. Check with VTech about how it behaves in an outage before counting on it.

items: A working phone line. These phones need a landline or a VoIP line (phone service over the internet). The phone's price does not include service, so check what the home has before ordering.
Loudness from the seller you buy from. Figures can differ between pages, so go by the number shown where you place the order.
Big, high-contrast buttons that are easy to see and press.
Photo or one-touch dialing. Handy, but someone has to set up the photos and numbers.
Power needs. Cordless bases need power, and the Clarity page says the P300 works during a power outage.
Return rules. Some sellers limit returns or charge a fee, so read the policy first.

No monthly fees. None of the phones below shows one on the pages we read; your phone service is separate. Prices vary by seller, and the P300 appeared anywhere from $74.95 to $129.99 across the pages reviewed, so check the order page.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well

Pick a spot near the chair where calls usually happen, with good light and an outlet or phone jack close by. For a cordless model, put the base somewhere central so the handset stays in range around the house.

Next, load the speed dial. This is a good job for a visiting son, daughter or neighbor: print small photos of family members, slip them into the photo buttons, and store each number. VTech's series page says its photo buttons "take the guesswork out of dialing." Make one test call to each button together.

Then adjust the sound. Try raising the volume during a real call, and try the tone control too, since a clearer voice is often more useful than a louder one. If the phone has a one-touch boost button, show where it is so it is easy to find mid-call.

The SN5127 and SN5147 pages list a smart call blocker with a 1,000-number block directory. It may help with repeat nuisance callers, but it will not stop every scam call, so the usual caution still applies: never give out bank or personal details to someone who called you.

Sources list the Clarity P300's call boost differently: ParentGiving says up to 18 dB, while Clarity's own page says up to 26 dB. Check the specs and price on the page where you actually order, and read the return policy, since ParentGiving does not accept returns under $79 in product value and charges a $3 return processing fee.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A louder, clearer phone will not fix everything, but it can turn calls back into something to look forward to. Pick the style that fits the home, set up those photo buttons together, and enjoy hearing the people you love a little better.

products.name: Clarity P300 Amplified Photo Phone
products.price: $89.99 sale, regular $99.99 at ParentGiving (check current price)
products.blurb: A corded desk or wall phone for someone who wants simple photo dialing, with 9 photo speed-dial buttons, a one-touch amplification button and an illuminated emergency button. Clarity's own page, not the ParentGiving listing, adds a 75+ dB ringer and says it works during a power outage.

products.name: VTech SN5127 Amplified Cordless Phone with Answering System
products.price: $69.95 at VTech (listed January 2026; check current price)
products.blurb: A cordless phone for someone who likes to move around the house, with 50-decibel Audio Assist, a 90-decibel ringer, up to eight one-touch photo numbers and a smart call blocker with a 1,000-number block directory. Extra SN5107 handsets are $38.95 each and need an SN5127 or SN5147 base.
